ideas.label: Ideas
ideas.placeholder: Type an idea — a library that lends tools instead of books
ideas.anchor: A library that lends tools instead of books.

blurb.image: Swaps one part for something else: a material, a person, a process, a rule, a place. Everything else stays.
blurb.ideas: Swaps one part for something else: a material, a person, a process, a rule, a place. Everything else stays.

example.image: The lamp is a beehive; the keeper tends the swarm at dusk.
example.ideas: Skill library: instead of a drill, you borrow an hour of the neighbor who knows how to use one.

blurb.image: Merges the concept with something else, often something unrelated, so the two become one thing.
blurb.ideas: Merges the concept with something else, often something unrelated, so the two become one thing.

example.image: A lighthouse grown into a tree: the lamp sits in the crown, roots grip the cliff.
example.ideas: Laundromat workshop: a tool library inside the laundromat, so you fix the chair while your clothes dry.

blurb.image: Borrows how another field, trade, creature or era solves things, and applies that here.
blurb.ideas: Borrows how another field, trade, creature or era solves things, and applies that here.

example.image: The lighthouse runs like an airport: a strip of landing lights down the cliff face.
example.ideas: Tool bank: run it like a blood bank; give a tool, bank a credit, draw any tool when you need one.

blurb.image: Changes one quality of the concept and pushes it hard: bigger, smaller, more often, louder, distorted.
blurb.ideas: Changes one quality of the concept and pushes it hard: bigger, smaller, more often, louder, distorted.

example.image: The lighthouse is ten storeys taller than the cliff; the beam sweeps the clouds, not the sea.
example.ideas: Street ritual: the library lends one tool a year, and the whole street votes on which.

blurb.image: Keeps the thing but gives it a different job. Same thing, new purpose.
blurb.ideas: Keeps the thing but gives it a different job. Same thing, new purpose.

example.image: The lighthouse is a cinema: its beam projects a film onto the fog.
example.ideas: Job exchange: borrow the ladder, and the fee is cleaning the gutters next door.

blurb.image: Takes something out. What's left shows what mattered.
blurb.ideas: Takes something out. What's left shows what mattered.

example.image: No lamp. A dark tower; ships steer by its silhouette against the stars.
example.ideas: Public repair bench: nothing leaves; the tools are chained to the bench and you bring the broken thing.

blurb.image: Flips an order or a direction: who does what to whom, cause and effect, inside and outside.
blurb.ideas: Flips an order or a direction: who does what to whom, cause and effect, inside and outside.

example.image: The sea sweeps a beam across the lighthouse; the tower is the thing being warned.
example.ideas: Reverse library: it borrows your idle tools and pays you back in free repairs.

blurb.image: Turns the concept into its opposite: what's missing instead of what's there, the empty space, the reverse situation.
blurb.ideas: Turns the concept into its opposite: what's missing instead of what's there, the empty space, the reverse situation.

example.image: A cliff with a lighthouse-shaped hole cut out of the night.
example.ideas: Museum of the unused: a catalog of tools people bought and never touched, open for borrowing.

blurb.image: Makes something enormously bigger or smaller than it should be, and keeps the rest the same.
blurb.ideas: Makes something enormously bigger or smaller than it should be, and keeps the rest the same.

example.image: A lighthouse the size of a thimble on the rim of a teacup; the beam crosses the saucer.
example.ideas: City-wide drill: one drill for the whole city, booked a year ahead, passed hand to hand.

blurb.image: Describes the concept as if seen for the first time, by someone who doesn't know the usual words for things.
blurb.ideas: Describes the concept as if seen for the first time, by someone who doesn't know the usual words for things.

example.image: A white stone finger on the edge of the land, blinking slowly at the dark water as if counting it.
example.ideas: Strangers hand each other heavy metal objects there, and bring them back a little worn.

blurb.image: Finds the one rule that makes this thing what it is, and breaks it. The thing stays recognizable, but wrong in one essential way.
blurb.ideas: Finds the one rule that makes this thing what it is, and breaks it. The thing stays recognizable, but wrong in one essential way.

example.image: A lighthouse built inland, in a wheat field, warning ships that can never come.
example.ideas: Pass-it-on library: nothing is ever returned; whatever you borrow is yours until someone else needs it.

blurb.image: States something impossible about the concept as if it were true, then follows it to a result.
blurb.ideas: States something impossible about the concept as if it were true, then follows it to a result.

example.image: The lighthouse is afraid of the dark; its beam never leaves its own feet.
example.ideas: Tool rating system: every tool logs who used it, and won't unlock for whoever last broke it.

moves.evidenceNote: Strong in the studio's tests, though Concretization after it cancelled its jolt.

blurb.image: Keeps how the parts of the concept relate to each other, and rebuilds it in a different world you name.
blurb.ideas: Keeps how the parts of the concept relate to each other, and rebuilds it in a different world you name.

example.image: → gardening: a sunflower at the edge of the field, its head turned to guide the bees home.
example.ideas: → cooking: Pan library: borrow a pan, return it with a portion of whatever you cooked in it.

moves.evidenceNote: Drifted under one judge in the studio's tests; a second judge rated it well.

blurb.image: Turns an abstract or poetic idea into a plain picture you could actually draw or photograph.
blurb.ideas: Turns an abstract or vague idea into a specific instance you could point at.

example.image: "loneliness, as a lighthouse" → One lit window in a lighthouse, a single chair turned to face the sea.
example.ideas: "generosity, as a public service" → Tool library with no sign-up: take what you need and chalk your name on the board.

blurb.image: Pulls A into B's world and lets B's logic change it, so the two genuinely intersect.
blurb.ideas: Pulls A into B's world and lets B's logic change it, so the two genuinely intersect.

example.image: A lighthouse × a vending machine → a coin slot in the lighthouse door; the beam turns once per coin.
example.ideas: Tool library × vending machine → Street vending machine: lends a drill for a coin and takes the broken one back.

moves.evidenceNote: The owner's favorite in the studio's blind picks; collisions beat single-concept moves in every test.

blurb.image: Breaks both concepts into their parts, picks the two parts that clash best, and collides just those.
blurb.ideas: Breaks both concepts into their parts, picks the two parts that clash best, and collides just those.

example.image: A lighthouse × a beehive → the beam's sweep × the swarm's hum: a lighthouse whose light pulses in time with bees.
example.ideas: Tool library × night bakery → lending × the early hours: a 4 a.m. counter where bakers lend their tools to the next shift.

moves.evidenceNote: In the studio, choosing what to collide first added non-obviousness; Split and pair then Bisociation was the owner's top recipe.

blurb.image: Finds the structure A and B share, then builds one new thing that takes from both and adds something neither had.
blurb.ideas: Finds the structure A and B share, then builds one new thing that takes from both and adds something neither had.

example.image: A lighthouse × a hourglass → a tower whose light drains down into the sea as the night passes.
example.ideas: Tool library × a time bank → Hour library: every tool comes with an hour of its owner's help, repaid in your own hours.

blurb.image: Keeps A mostly as it is and plants one charged piece of B inside it, as a single anomaly that takes over.
blurb.ideas: Keeps A mostly as it is and plants one charged piece of B inside it, as a single anomaly that takes over.

example.image: A lighthouse, with B = a bird's nest → the lamp room is one enormous nest; the keeper climbs in through twigs.
example.ideas: Tool library, with B = a confessional → the return desk is a booth: you confess what you broke, and nobody fines you.

moves.evidenceNote: Strong in the studio's tests; the most reliable second step after another collision.

blurb.image: Finds where the two concepts' logics meet and grows one new idea there, with both parents still visible.
blurb.ideas: Finds where the two concepts' logics meet and grows one new idea there, with both parents still visible.

example.image: A lighthouse × a snow globe → a lighthouse sealed in glass, its beam caught swirling in the snow.
example.ideas: Tool library × a confession booth → Tool return booth: you hand back the tool and confess what you broke with it.

blurb.image: Treats A and B as opposites, finds the real contradiction between them, and resolves it into a third thing.
blurb.ideas: Treats A and B as opposites, finds the real contradiction between them, and resolves it into a third thing.

example.image: A lighthouse × a fog bank → a tower that gives off fog instead of light, so ships steer by where it hides.
example.ideas: Tool library × a hoarder's garage → Keep-forever library: you never return a tool, you lend it onward and it keeps a trail.

moves.evidenceNote: Judges disagreed in the studio: last under one, mid-pack under another. It can wander.

blurb.image: Climbs from the thing to what it is an example of: its category, its job, the principle behind it.
blurb.ideas: Climbs from the thing to what it is an example of: its category, its job, the principle behind it.

example.image: A lighthouse → a single eye kept open all night over a sleeping coast.
example.ideas: A tool library → Shared-capability network: any building on the street can lend whatever it is best equipped for.

blurb.image: Climbs down to one specific, named instance in a particular time and place.
blurb.ideas: Climbs down to one specific, named instance in a particular time and place.

example.image: A lighthouse → the Eddystone lighthouse in 1759, its lamp a ring of twenty-four tallow candles.
example.ideas: A tool library → the 2010 Berkeley Tool Lending Library: a basement counter, a membership card, a waiting list for the tile saw.

moves.evidenceNote: In the studio it grounded collisions well but cancelled the jolt of a Provocation.

blurb.image: Lets one part stand for the whole, or the whole stand for one part.
blurb.ideas: Lets one part stand for the whole, or the whole stand for one part.

example.image: A lighthouse → only the turning lens, alone on the cliff, still throwing its light.
example.ideas: A tool library → Library card: one card that unlocks any garage on the street for a single hour.

blurb.image: Swaps the thing for something next to it: what it touches, causes, uses or sits beside.
blurb.ideas: Swaps the thing for something next to it: what it touches, causes, uses or sits beside.

example.image: A lighthouse → the keeper's logbook open on the table, lit by a beam that sweeps in through the window.
example.ideas: A tool library → Sawdust exchange: the library trades in what tools leave behind, sawdust, offcuts, spare screws.

blurb.image: Replaces the thing with something from a different world that has the same feeling or job.
blurb.ideas: Replaces the thing with something from a different world that has the same feeling or job.

example.image: A lighthouse → an old conductor on a cliff, baton raised, keeping the ships in time.
example.ideas: A tool library → Seed bank for skills: tools are stored like seeds, and each loan must come back with a cutting of what you made.

blurb.image: Digs up the old, literal meaning of a key word and builds the concept on that.
blurb.ideas: Digs up the old, literal meaning of a key word and builds the concept on that.

example.image: A lighthouse ('pharos', from the island of Pharos) → an island that is itself the lamp, glowing from the rock up.
example.ideas: A tool library ('library', from Latin liber, the inner bark of a tree) → Bark library: tools lent from a hollow oak in the park.

blurb.image: Carries the concept through other languages and keeps whatever the meaning drifts into.
blurb.ideas: Carries the concept through other languages and keeps whatever the meaning drifts into.

example.image: A lighthouse, through Japanese and back → a 'tower of the lamp-guardian': a tower that guards a single lamp from the sea.
example.ideas: A tool library, through German and back → 'Werkzeugleihe', a lending of work: you borrow the job, and the tools come with it.

blurb.image: Works out the rule that could have produced the concept, then lets the rule make new ones.
blurb.ideas: Works out the rule that could have produced the concept, then lets the rule make new ones.

example.image: A lighthouse ([Rule: a tall thing that turns to watch over a dark flat]) → a giraffe at the edge of a night savanna, head slowly sweeping.
example.ideas: A tool library ([Rule: lend what people own but rarely use]) → a wedding-dress library run by a church hall.

blurb.image: Gets to the concept by misusing a tool, medium or system for something it was never meant to do.
blurb.ideas: Gets to the concept by misusing a tool, medium or system for something it was never meant to do.

example.image: A lighthouse → a lighthouse drawn by leaving a long-exposure camera on a ship's mast through one stormy night.
example.ideas: A tool library → Library run on a parcel locker network: tools travel by courier between neighbors, the lockers are the shelves.

blurb.image: Recasts the concept as its own paperwork: the receipt, instruction, certificate or trace of something absent.
blurb.ideas: Recasts the concept as its own paperwork: the receipt, instruction, certificate or trace of something absent.

example.image: A lighthouse → a keeper's logbook page: 'Lamp lit 18:04. No ships. Lamp lit for no one again.'
example.ideas: A tool library → Loan slips as the archive: every slip records what was built with the tool, and the slips are the exhibit.

blurb.image: Breaks the concept into its parts and builds on one part at a time.
blurb.ideas: Breaks the concept into its parts and builds on one part at a time.

example.image: A lighthouse → just its rhythm: a coastline where every fourth wave breaks in light.
example.ideas: A tool library → just its return date: a service that reminds you what you meant to finish before you borrowed it.

blurb.image: Imposes one rule the whole concept must obey, and lets obeying it reshape everything.
blurb.ideas: Imposes one rule the whole concept must obey, and lets obeying it reshape everything.

example.image: A lighthouse, rule: everything is wet → a lighthouse whose beam is a falling sheet of water lit from within.
example.ideas: A tool library, rule: nothing may leave the building → Repair hall: you bring the broken thing in, the tools never travel.

field.name: rule
field.label: The rule
field.placeholder: a rule to impose (optional) — everything is wet

blurb.image: Finds what the concept or its medium does best, and refuses it.
blurb.ideas: Finds what the concept or its medium does best, and refuses it.

example.image: A lighthouse that refuses light: a dark tower ships find by its sound, a slow bell in the fog.
example.ideas: A tool library that refuses lending → Tool museum: you may only watch the tools being used, by their owners.

blurb.image: Writes the concept under a word game, like no letter E, and keeps the odd idea the game forces.
blurb.ideas: Writes the concept under a word game, like no letter E, and keeps the odd idea the game forces.

example.image: A lighthouse without the letter E → a tall stone pillar lit at its top; a gull holds a lamp in its jaws.
example.ideas: A tool library, one vowel only → 'Stock shop of tools': a shop where you swap a tool for a job, not for cash.

blurb.image: Draws a random card from Eno and Schmidt's deck of oblique directives and applies it to the concept.
blurb.ideas: Draws a random card from Eno and Schmidt's deck of oblique directives and applies it to the concept.

example.image: A lighthouse, card 'Water' → a lighthouse standing in a puddle, its whole beam reflected downward.
example.ideas: A tool library, card 'Use an old idea' → the 19th-century lending guild, rebuilt as a phone app.

blurb.image: Free-associates from the concept like automatic writing, and keeps the strangeness.
blurb.ideas: Free-associates from the concept like automatic writing, and keeps the strangeness.

example.image: A lighthouse → the lamp dreams of moths; at dawn the tower is full of them, sleeping in rows on the glass.
example.ideas: A tool library → a hammer goes out on loan and comes back as a key; the library now lends whatever comes back.

blurb.image: Keeps only the last word or image of the concept and starts a brand-new idea from it.
blurb.ideas: Keeps only the last word or image of the concept and starts a brand-new idea from it.

example.image: A lighthouse on a cliff → (cliff) a cliff face lined with doorbells; nobody knows who lives inside.
example.ideas: A library that lends tools instead of books → (books) Books lent by the gram: you pay for what you actually read.

blurb.image: Tells the same concept from someone or something else in it: a witness, an object, an animal.
blurb.ideas: Tells the same concept from someone or something else in it: a witness, an object, an animal.

example.image: A lighthouse, as the moth on the glass sees it: a sun that turns away every nine seconds.
example.ideas: A tool library, from the drill's side → Tool diaries: each tool keeps a log of every house it has worked in.

blurb.image: Moves the concept to a different era, with that era's objects and logic, keeping its core.
blurb.ideas: Moves the concept to a different era, with that era's objects and logic, keeping its core.

example.image: A lighthouse in 1200 → a monk with a fire basket on a church tower, ringing for the fishing boats.
example.ideas: A tool library in 2090 → Fabrication library: you borrow a file, the street's printer makes the tool, then melts it back.

blurb.image: Keeps the same concept but changes its feeling: tender to sinister, solemn to comic.
blurb.ideas: Keeps the same concept but changes its feeling: tender to sinister, solemn to comic.

example.image: A lighthouse, sinister → the beam pauses on each boat a moment too long, as if counting who is aboard.
example.ideas: A tool library, comic → Tool library with a strict librarian: overdue hammers get a public notice in the newsletter.

blurb.image: Squeezes the concept down to its single essential core, and lets the rest go.
blurb.ideas: Squeezes the concept down to its single essential core, and lets the rest go.

example.image: A lighthouse on a cliff → one lit window, high up, in the dark.
example.ideas: A library that lends tools instead of books → Borrow, don't buy: one shared shelf per street.
